strengths: The paper addresses a relevant limitation of classification-based Bayesian optimization: excessive concentration around previously promising regions. Combining BORE-style classification with label propagation or label spreading is a useful, well-motivated contribution, particularly when candidate pools provide meaningful geometric information.

The evaluation includes continuous and finite-pool synthetic problems, hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and an image-embedding search task. Comparisons against multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers and GP-based methods, with 20 repetitions and standard errors, provide substantial empirical evidence. Figures 2 and 6 show particularly promising improvements.

The appendices investigate kernel parameters, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, pool subsampling, and threshold ratios. These analyses expose important sensitivities and include a valuable comparison against the corresponding model without unlabeled data.

The relationship to BORE, LFBO, and established graph-based semi-supervised learning is explained adequately. The pseudocode and benchmark specifications help readers understand the approach, and Appendix C appropriately acknowledges limitations of transferring existing theory to sequential optimization.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not sufficiently isolated experimentally. Figure 12 shows that removing unlabeled data can match or outperform the proposed variants, notably on Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. However, this ablation fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main experiments learn beta. A comparably tuned Nadaraya–Watson baseline using identical acquisition optimization and tie-breaking is needed to establish whether the main gains come from unlabeled-data propagation. This unresolved attribution is the primary reason for recommending weak rejection.

The explanation for improved exploration remains insufficiently supported. Sampling truncated Gaussians around observed points does not establish the cluster assumption: high-density connections can cross boundaries between objective-derived labels, which also change during optimization. Appendix C does not demonstrate that propagation expands the promising region or that such expansion improves optimization. The illustrative trajectories and inapplicable i.i.d. learning bounds provide intuition, but stronger measurements of exploration or narrower claims are needed.

Several consequential implementation details remain unclear: input scaling and categorical encoding, the initialization and bounds for learning beta, label-spreading and convergence settings, and complete GP/MLP training configurations. The stated L-BFGS-B procedure also leaves acquisition maximization over finite candidate pools insufficiently explained. These choices affect graph geometry, baseline performance, and reproducibility.

The evidence for general applicability is limited. All continuous benchmarks are two-dimensional. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses representations trained on 440,000 labeled examples of the same digit-recognition task. This is a legitimate shared representation, but it tests a particularly informative geometry; comparison with direct ranking by the pretrained classifier and additional high-dimensional problems would clarify its significance.

The computational tradeoff is not established against competing methods. Figure 14 measures sensitivity to pool size, but does not compare complete optimization overhead, including repeated bandwidth learning and acquisition optimization. Random search and a simple randomized-exploration modification of BORE would also provide useful controls for the proposed exploration benefit.

A correctable mathematical inconsistency affects the algorithm description: the column-normalized definition of p_ij implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas Section 4.1 states P = D^{-1} W. This should be reconciled with the transpose in Equation 11 so the intended propagation update is unambiguous.
